title: Laws for the Land, Defiant Sin, and Tassels of Blue
summary: Right after the refusal at Kadesh, God gives laws for life in the land: grain and drink offerings to go with every sacrifice, and a loaf from the first of the dough. He provides offerings for sins committed in error, by the whole community or by one person, but none for sin done in open defiance. A man caught gathering wood on the Sabbath is put to death, and Israel is told to wear tassels with a blue cord as a reminder to keep God's commands.
story: Chapter 14 ended in disaster. The people refused to enter Canaan, God sentenced the adult generation to die in the wilderness over forty years, and an unauthorized attack on the hill country ended in a rout as far as Hormah. Chapter 15 opens, with no transition at all, on laws that begin “After you enter the land that I am giving you as a home” (verse 2). Placed here, that clause is a promise. The generation that refused will not see the land, but their children will, and God is already telling them what to bring from its grain, oil, and wine. The chapter then turns to sin: how it can be atoned for when it is unintended, why no offering is named when it is defiant, and what defiance looked like in one man's case. It closes with tassels meant to keep Israel's eyes on God's commands rather than on its own desires, which is exactly where the scouts had gone wrong. Chapter 16 follows with Korah's rebellion, the largest challenge yet to Moses and Aaron.
historical:
No date or place is attached to these laws beyond the wilderness setting of verse 32, and their position right after Kadesh is their real setting. The offerings assume a settled farming life. Grain, olive oil, and wine were the three staples of Canaan's agriculture, and a people living on manna in the desert would not have had them in any quantity, so the law looks ahead to fields, olive groves, and vineyards Israel does not yet hold. The measures are the ephah, a dry measure for grain, and the hin, a liquid measure for oil and wine. Their exact sizes are uncertain and modern estimates vary, but the scale is clear: the larger the animal, the larger the offering that goes with it (a tenth of an ephah of flour for a lamb, two-tenths for a ram, three-tenths for a bull).

Scholars who trace the Pentateuch to several sources usually assign this chapter to its priestly material, and some note that its closing call to be holy resembles the Holiness Code of Leviticus 17 to 26. Those who read the Torah as substantially Mosaic see deliberate placement: laws for the land given to a people who had just refused it. Readers on both sides notice that Numbers 15 supplements Leviticus rather than repeating it. Leviticus 2 treats the grain offering as a gift on its own; here it accompanies every animal sacrifice. And in Leviticus 4 the congregation's unintentional sin requires a young bull as a sin offering, while here the bull is a burnt offering and a male goat is the sin offering. Interpreters explain the difference in several ways, among them that Leviticus has in view doing what was forbidden while Numbers has in view failing to do all that was commanded (verse 22), or that the two texts reflect different stages of Israel's practice.
cultural:
The first thing a modern reader needs is the difference between unintentional and defiant sin. The Hebrew word for the first covers wrongs done by mistake or in ignorance, and the sacrificial system was built to deal with them: an animal offered, the priest making atonement, and the promise that the offender will be forgiven. Defiant sin is described with an idiom, literally sinning with a raised hand, the picture of a fist lifted against God. No offering is prescribed for it. The person is to be cut off, a penalty whose meaning is debated: some take it as execution by the community, others as premature death or the ending of a family line at God's hand, and later Jewish tradition generally understood it as a punishment God himself carries out.

The Sabbath law was already known. Work on the seventh day carried the death penalty (Exodus 31:14-15), and kindling a fire at home on the Sabbath had been singled out (Exodus 35:3). The man gathering wood was presumably preparing a fire. The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13), so open contempt for it was contempt for the covenant. The tassels belong to the world of clothing as identity. Decorated hems appear on the garments of important people in ancient Near Eastern art, and a hem could stand for its owner (compare David cutting the corner of Saul's robe in 1 Samuel 24). The blue cord used the color of the tabernacle's curtains and the high priest's robe, a costly dye made in the ancient world from Mediterranean sea snails, so every Israelite's clothing carried a thread of the sanctuary's color. Jewish men still wear tassels called tzitzit, often all white because the method of making the biblical blue was lost for centuries, and verses 37 to 41 became the third paragraph of the Shema, the confession recited morning and evening in Jewish prayer.
literary: Numbers often interrupts its story with law, and this chapter is a clear case. It gathers four blocks of legislation and one story, and the order is purposeful. The first two laws (verses 1-21) look forward to life in the land. The next section moves from forgivable error to defiance that no sacrifice covers (verses 22-31), and the story of the Sabbath-breaker (verses 32-36) follows at once as a case of defiance. The chapter closes with a remedy for the wandering heart (verses 37-41). Two refrains bind it together. One is the equality of native Israelite and resident foreigner, repeated in verses 14-16, 26, 29, and 30. The other is the phrase “for the generations to come”, which assumes a future for a people just condemned to die. The Sabbath-breaker's case also belongs to a small group of stories in the Torah where Moses must wait for God to rule on something the law had not yet settled (compare Leviticus 24:10-23; Numbers 9:6-14; 27:1-11). The tassel law ends with God's own signature, “I am the LORD your God”, spoken twice in verse 41.

outline.t: Grain and drink offerings with every sacrifice, one law for native and foreigner
Unintentional sin of the whole congregation
Defiant sin: no offering, cut off
The man gathering wood on the Sabbath
Tassels with a blue cord to remember the commandments

doctrines.note: Atonement is God's provision, not Israel's achievement: the priest makes atonement, and the people are forgiven (verses 25-28). The chapter also shows the system's limit. For the one who sins defiantly no offering is named, and “his guilt remains on him” (verse 31).

Scripture distinguishes sins of weakness and ignorance from sin that is open rebellion. Defiance is treated as more than breaking a rule: the defiant sinner “blasphemes the LORD” and has “despised the word of the LORD” (verses 30-31). Sin at its root is contempt for God himself.

The tassels exist so that Israel will remember and obey, and “you will be holy to your God” (verse 40). Holiness is not reserved for priests. A thread of the sanctuary's blue on every household's clothing claims the whole people for God.

God's law binds native Israelite and resident foreigner alike: “You and the foreigner shall be the same before the LORD” (verse 15). The law is also given with a future in view, for the generations to come, to a people who have just forfeited their own entry into the land.

words.note: Shegagah, error or inadvertence. It names a wrong done by mistake or without knowing, and it appears seven times in this chapter. The whole sacrificial provision of verses 22-29 depends on it. Its opposite in verse 30 is not a single word but an idiom, sinning with a raised hand, and the contrast between the two frames everything the chapter says about forgiveness.

Salach, to forgive or pardon. In the Hebrew Bible God is always the subject of this verb; people are never said to salach one another. It is the word Moses used when he begged God to pardon the people in 14:19 and God answered that he had pardoned them (14:20). Here it is promised three times to those who bring an offering for unintentional sin.

Tur, to seek out or explore. It is the verb used for the scouts who spied out the land in chapters 13 and 14. In verse 39 it describes following one's own heart and eyes, which the BSB renders “following”. The echo is pointed: the scouts went looking with their own eyes and came back with unbelief, and the tassels are given so that Israel will look at God's commands instead.

Tsitsit, tassel or fringe. The word gives its name to the tassels Jewish men still wear. Each was to carry a blue cord and hang from the corners of an outer garment, a reminder at the edge of ordinary clothing that the wearer belonged to the LORD and was bound to his commands.

christ: The New Testament picks up several of this chapter's threads. The letter to the Hebrews builds on the distinction between unintentional and defiant sin. It describes the high priest as one who can deal gently with the ignorant and misguided because he shares their weakness (Hebrews 5:2), and it warns that for those who go on sinning deliberately after receiving the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains (Hebrews 10:26-29), language that echoes the one who despised the word of the LORD. Hebrews presents Jesus as the priest whose single offering accomplishes what the repeated sacrifices pointed toward. On the cross Jesus prayed for those who crucified him because they did not know what they were doing (Luke 23:34, a verse missing from some early manuscripts), and Peter told the crowd in Jerusalem that they had acted in ignorance before calling them to repent (Acts 3:17-19). The tassels appear in the Gospels as well: the sick reached for the fringe of Jesus' cloak to be healed (Matthew 9:20; 14:36), and he rebuked teachers who lengthened their tassels for show (Matthew 23:5). The single law for Israelite and foreigner is a thematic link rather than a prediction, but it points toward the church, where Gentiles are no longer strangers but members of God's household (Ephesians 2:19).

hard.q: Why was a man put to death for gathering sticks on the Sabbath?
hard.a:
The penalty is severe by any measure, and the text does not soften it. The man speaks no word, and we are told nothing of his motives. Interpreters point to several things. The first is placement: the story comes directly after the law on defiant sin, and most readers take it as an example of sin with a raised hand rather than a mistake. The Sabbath was no obscure rule. Israel had been taught it with the manna (Exodus 16) and told its penalty (Exodus 31), so this was likely a public act of defiance. The second is the Sabbath's meaning: it was the sign of the covenant, and in a camp where God himself dwelt as king, openly breaking it was treated as treason rather than a private lapse. The third is restraint: the community did not act on impulse but held the man in custody and waited for God's ruling.

Many readers find these answers true but incomplete, and the story stays hard. Christians have generally held that Israel's civil penalties belonged to its unique situation as a nation under God's direct rule and are not a model for the church, whose discipline stops at exclusion (1 Corinthians 5). Jesus kept the Sabbath while opposing rules that made it a burden, saying the Sabbath was made for people and that he is Lord of it (Mark 2:27-28), and Paul calls the Sabbath a shadow of what was to come in Christ (Colossians 2:16-17). Christians differ on how the Sabbath command applies now, but none reads this story as a pattern for civil punishment today. What it still presses on the reader is that God is not indifferent to being defied.

questions: God gave laws for life in the land to a generation he had just told would die in the wilderness. What does it say about him that his instructions came with a promise attached?
The chapter distinguishes wrongs done in error from wrongs done in open defiance. Why does that distinction matter, and where is it hard for you to be honest about which one you are committing?
The tassels were worn so that people would not follow their own heart and eyes. What reminders or practices keep you from drifting wherever your eyes pull you?
